b:
"Whatever else you guard, guard your tongue"

We are vegetarians by birth.. When we say it, pride comes running from somewhere and sticks to us. If we saw a six-foot fish cart we'd walk eight feet away. We'd only wet our hands in vegetarian homes.. otherwise something would come from somewhere and stick to us..

That was our previous generation.

We are still vegetarian today. As long as nobody tells us there is egg in the cake, we can eat it.. Our days go by in the faith that vegetarian food is cooked separately in non-vegetarian restaurants.

The next generation will go past us.

I am no enemy of meat.. I never got used to it.. After a certain age I didn't want to get used to it. That's all.

Beyond vegetarian or not, I am one who believes that in this eight-span body, the belly is chief

My mother's cooking never pushed me to look beyond vegetarian food.. Every day our house had all kinds of curries, like a feast.. and the peak of it was colour-colour papad.. Like a doubled word, it sticks to the tongue. As a child, when we went to the grocery shop, my head would go cool just watching them pinch it off into the bag.

At home, a little game with Amma and the boiling oil.. The first papad dropped in to test the heat would lie flat in the oil with a hiss.. Amma would laugh at me for dropping it in even after being told the oil wasn't hot yet.. Then each of the colours I had counted out in a row would take its bath in the oil one after another and laugh.. As I crushed each one and buried it in rice and ate, there was joy on one side.. and on the other the sorrow that the papads were running out

The only taste to equal the colour-colour papads was my aunt's sago papad.. Once or twice a year they would pack it and send it from Araly just for me.. As the years went on the parcels shrank and disappeared altogether.. As the saying goes, "don't leave your husband trusting in the king"; the colour-colour papads stood by me

A newspaper snippet from somewhere planted a fear of cancer in my mother, and from that day those papads were banished from the house.. The sudden ban left me deflated.. Later they disappeared from the shops too..

The fried plantain chips and pappadams that came in their place filled my stomach but did not soothe my heart.. Every time I tear a tearing pappadam I hear the laughter of my colour-colour papads
note: The opening is Thirukkural 127, "guard your tongue" (meaning your speech), here turned into a joke about taste. "In this eight-span body, the belly is chief" twists the proverb "the head is chief". "Colour-colour" is a doubled word, the kind Tamil grammar calls irattaik kilavi, which cannot be split apart. Araly is a village near Jaffna.
